title: Hybrid Connectivity: VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute and Virtual WAN (Advanced)
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Choose between site-to-site VPN, point-to-site VPN, VNet-to-VNet, ExpressRoute and Virtual WAN for a requirement.
- Explain how a route-based VPN gateway is built: GatewaySubnet, public IP, local network gateway, connection, IPsec/IKE, BGP and active-active.
- Pick a current VPN Gateway SKU, and an ExpressRoute circuit SKU, billing model and resiliency level.
- Plan non-overlapping address space for head office, forty stores, remote users and Azure.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

The new orders API runs in Azure on 10.40.0.0/16, but the warehouse system and the finance database still live in Pak Budi's server room at head office in Jakarta, on 10.0.0.0/16. Today the two talk through a public endpoint protected by an IP allow list that Pak Budi edits by hand. The forty stores upload the day's sales every night across the internet. During the last 12.12 sale, one store's upload failed three nights in a row, and nobody noticed until finance tried to close the month.

Pak Budi wants "a proper private line". Ibu Sari wants to know three things: is it private, what happens when the line goes down, and what will it cost every month?

Today's question: which private path should connect head office and the stores to Azure — and how do you keep it up when one link fails?

Reading

1. Why hybrid, and the three families of connections

Hybrid networking joins networks you run yourself — head office, stores, a datacenter — to virtual networks in Azure, so that machines reach each other on private IP addresses as if they shared one network. Nusantara Retail needs it because migration is gradual: the warehouse system stays at head office for at least another year, while every new service lands in Azure.

Azure offers three families of hybrid connectivity:

- VPN Gateway builds encrypted tunnels across the public internet. It's quick to set up, cheap to start and works wherever there is an internet connection.
- ExpressRoute is a private connection into Microsoft's network through a connectivity provider. It never crosses the public internet and performs predictably, but ordering one takes weeks.
- Virtual WAN is a Microsoft-managed hub that combines VPN, ExpressRoute and virtual network connections at scale, for organisations with many sites.

Plan the addresses first. Every hybrid design breaks if two connected networks use the same addresses: no router can tell which 10.0.1.10 you mean. As in Lunch 08, pick ranges that will never collide and write them down before anyone builds anything. Nusantara Retail's plan:

Network | Address space | Notes
Head office (Jakarta) | 10.0.0.0/16 | Pak Budi's existing network; it can't change
Azure hub and workloads | 10.40.0.0/16 | The gateway subnets live here
Stores | 10.100.0.0/16 | One /24 per store (10.100.1.0/24 to 10.100.40.0/24), with room to grow
Point-to-site clients | 172.16.200.0/24 | Addresses handed to VPN users' laptops

If an overlap can't be avoided — say Nusantara Retail buys a company whose network also uses 10.0.0.0/16 — VPN Gateway can translate one side's addresses with NAT rules. Treat that as a last resort: it makes troubleshooting and DNS harder.

Plan name resolution, too. A working tunnel is only half the job; names must resolve on both sides. Azure's built-in DNS at 168.63.129.16 answers only from inside Azure virtual networks, so head-office servers can't query it across a VPN. The usual answer is Azure DNS Private Resolver in the hub (Lunch 25): its inbound endpoint lets Pak Budi's DNS servers forward lookups for Azure private zones into Azure, and its outbound endpoint, with a forwarding ruleset, sends lookups for head office's internal domain back to his DNS servers.

2. VPN Gateway: encrypted tunnels over the internet

A VPN gateway is a set of Microsoft-managed instances that Azure deploys into a special subnet of your virtual network, the GatewaySubnet. The name must be exactly GatewaySubnet, nothing else may live in it, and you must not attach a network security group to it. Microsoft recommends /27 or larger, which leaves room for later additions such as an ExpressRoute gateway alongside. The gateway gets a Standard public IP address: the address the on-premises device connects to.

Two more resources complete a site-to-site setup:

- A local network gateway describes the other side: the public IP address of Pak Budi's VPN device and the address ranges behind it (10.0.0.0/16), or its BGP settings.
- A connection joins the virtual network gateway to the local network gateway and holds the authentication — usually a pre-shared key that both sides must know; certificate-based authentication is also available.

Inside the tunnel, IKE (Internet Key Exchange) negotiates keys and IPsec encrypts every packet. Azure's default IPsec/IKE policies suit most devices, and you can set a custom policy when a security team requires specific algorithms.

How a tunnel comes up. First the two ends use IKE to prove that they share the same key (or trust each other's certificates) and to agree on algorithms; the result is an IKE security association. Over that protected channel they negotiate IPsec security associations, which carry the actual traffic, and they renew the keys on a schedule. Only when both phases succeed does the connection status change from Connecting to Connected. Most failed tunnels come from a mismatch: a different pre-shared key, algorithms the device doesn't accept, or address ranges that don't line up. Your first diagnostics are the connection status and its ingress and egress byte counters; for harder cases, Network Watcher's VPN troubleshoot and the gateway's packet capture show what each side proposed.

Route-based or policy-based? A route-based gateway sends any traffic that matches its routes into the tunnel; a policy-based gateway encrypts only traffic between fixed address pairs. Choose route-based: point-to-site, BGP, active-active and VNet-to-VNet all need it, and policy-based is offered only on the Basic SKU. An older firewall that speaks only policy-based VPN can still connect to a route-based gateway with policy-based traffic selectors.

Active-active and BGP. By default a gateway runs active-standby: one instance carries the tunnels and the other takes over during maintenance or a failure, with a short interruption. In active-active mode each instance has its own public IP and carries its own tunnel, so failover is much smoother; it's the recommended production setup. BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) lets the gateway and Pak Budi's router exchange routes automatically instead of you typing prefixes into the local network gateway, and it makes multiple tunnels and transit routing work. Azure VPN gateways use the private AS number 65515 unless you choose another.

One gateway for many VNets. In a hub-and-spoke network (Lunch 25), only the hub needs a gateway. Turn on Allow gateway transit on the hub's side of each peering and Use remote gateways on the spoke's side, and every spoke reaches head office through the hub's VPN or ExpressRoute gateway — one gateway to pay for and monitor. Azure adds the on-premises prefixes to every subnet's routes automatically, with virtual network gateway as the next hop; you'll see exactly such a route in the lab.

Three kinds of VPN connection share the same gateway:

Type | Connects | Nusantara Retail use | Authentication | Watch out for
Site-to-site (S2S) | An on-premises network to a VNet, through a VPN device with a public IP | Head office now, stores later | Pre-shared key or certificates | The device must be compatible; internet quality limits performance
Point-to-site (P2S) | One computer to a VNet, through a VPN client | Pak Budi working from home; Rizky reaching a private VM | Microsoft Entra ID, certificates or RADIUS | Entra ID needs OpenVPN and the Azure VPN Client, and isn't available on the Basic SKU; the client pool must not overlap
VNet-to-VNet | Two virtual networks, through a gateway in each | Encrypted links between regions; this lunch's lab | Pre-shared key | For Azure-to-Azure traffic, VNet peering (Lunch 25) is usually cheaper and faster

Point-to-site with Microsoft Entra ID authentication is the modern choice for staff: people sign in with their normal account, so MFA and Conditional Access apply, and there are no client certificates to issue and revoke. The Azure VPN Client runs on Windows and macOS.

Patience is part of the design. Creating a VPN gateway often takes 45 minutes or more, and some changes, such as switching to active-active, take a while too. Plan gateway changes in advance; don't click and wait.

3. VPN Gateway SKUs in 2026

The gateway SKU sets throughput, the number of tunnels and connections, and the features you get. The line-up changed recently, so older tutorials can mislead you:

- Since 1 November 2025 you can't create the old non-zonal VpnGw1–5 SKUs. Existing ones move to their zonal equivalents, and the old SKUs are deprecated from 30 September 2026. The legacy Standard and HighPerformance SKUs went even earlier, on 30 September 2025.
- The AZ SKUs, VpnGw1AZ to VpnGw5AZ, are the ones to use for every new gateway. In a region with availability zones the gateway is zone-redundant; in a region without zones it is deployed regionally.
- Basic still exists and isn't retiring, but it's for dev/test only: no BGP, no IKEv2 or OpenVPN for point-to-site, no RADIUS and no IPv6. It needs a Standard public IP and can only be created with PowerShell or the CLI.

SKU | Generation | Site-to-site tunnels (max) | Use it for
Basic | 1 | 10 | Dev/test and proofs of concept only
VpnGw1AZ | 1 | 30 | Small production: one head office and a few branches
VpnGw2AZ, VpnGw3AZ | 1 or 2 | 30 | More throughput and more point-to-site users
VpnGw4AZ, VpnGw5AZ | 2 | 100 | Large estates; beyond 100 tunnels, use Virtual WAN

At the time of writing, Microsoft's aggregate throughput benchmarks run from about 650 Mbps for VpnGw1AZ to 10 Gbps for VpnGw5AZ. They are benchmarks, not guarantees, and a single tunnel gets less, so check the SKU page and test with your own traffic. A gateway bills for every hour it exists, from the moment creation starts, whether or not traffic flows, and data leaving Azure is charged on top. There is no pause button: to stop paying, you delete the gateway.

Warning: The CLI's default SKU is Basic. az network vnet-gateway create without --sku quietly creates a Basic gateway — no BGP, no Entra ID for point-to-site, dev/test support only. Always pass --sku (for example VpnGw1AZ). Two more classic mistakes: putting a network security group or a 0.0.0.0/0 route on the GatewaySubnet, and connecting networks whose address spaces overlap.

4. ExpressRoute: a private line into Microsoft's network

ExpressRoute connects your network to Microsoft through a connectivity provider, such as a telco or an exchange, at an ExpressRoute location (also called a peering location): a colocation facility where Microsoft's edge routers sit. Jakarta has several at the time of writing, including a Jakarta Metro option. Traffic goes from Pak Budi's router across the provider's network to Microsoft's edge, without touching the public internet.

- The circuit is the logical connection, identified by a service key — a GUID you hand to the provider, not a secret. Every circuit has two connections to two Microsoft edge routers for built-in redundancy, and routes are exchanged with BGP. Bandwidths through providers range from 50 Mbps to 10 Gbps.
- Azure private peering reaches your virtual networks on private addresses through an ExpressRoute gateway in the VNet (ErGw1Az, ErGw2Az, ErGw3Az or the scalable ErGwScale). Microsoft peering reaches Microsoft's public services, such as Azure PaaS endpoints and, in specific scenarios, Microsoft 365, over public addresses you own.
- Circuit SKUs: Local (only Azure regions near the peering location, data transfer included in the port price), Standard (all regions in the same geopolitical area) and Premium (worldwide, with more routes and more VNet links). Billing is metered (pay per GB going out) or unlimited (flat fee); you can switch from metered to unlimited but not back.
- ExpressRoute Direct skips the provider: dual 10, 100 or 400 Gbps ports straight into Microsoft's network.
- Global Reach links your own sites to each other through their circuits over Microsoft's backbone. FastPath sends traffic straight to the VMs, bypassing the gateway (it needs ErGw3Az or ErGwScale).

Ordering a circuit follows a fixed sequence. You create the circuit in Azure — provider, peering location, bandwidth, SKU and billing model — and receive its service key. The provider uses the key to provision its side, and the circuit's provider status changes to Provisioned. Then you (or the provider) configure Azure private peering with BGP, create an ExpressRoute gateway in the hub's GatewaySubnet, and link the virtual network to the circuit with a connection. Virtual networks in other subscriptions can be linked too, using an authorization that the circuit's owner creates.

Resiliency comes in three levels. Standard resiliency is one circuit at one location: two connections, but one building. High resiliency, ExpressRoute Metro, splits one circuit across two sites in the same city. Maximum resiliency uses two circuits at two different peering locations — Microsoft's recommendation for critical workloads. Many organisations also keep a site-to-site VPN as a backup path, because VPN and ExpressRoute gateways can coexist in the same virtual network.

Important: Private is not the same as encrypted. ExpressRoute keeps traffic off the internet, but it doesn't encrypt it by default. When data must be encrypted in transit, use TLS in the application, MACsec on ExpressRoute Direct, or an IPsec VPN over the private peering.

| Site-to-site VPN | ExpressRoute
Path | Encrypted tunnel across the public internet | Private connection through a provider; never on the internet
Encryption | IPsec, always | Not by default (add TLS, MACsec or IPsec)
Bandwidth | Up to the gateway SKU's throughput, shared by all tunnels | 50 Mbps to 10 Gbps per circuit; up to 400 Gbps ports with Direct
Latency and jitter | Varies with the internet | Predictable
Time to set up | Hours, plus 45 minutes or more for the gateway | Weeks, while a provider provisions the circuit
Cost model | Gateway per hour, plus outbound data | Circuit per month (plus data if metered), gateway per hour, provider fees
Redundancy | Active-active gateway, two on-premises devices | Two connections per circuit; Metro or a second location for more
Best for | Getting started, small sites, a backup path | Heavy, steady, business-critical traffic

5. Virtual WAN: hubs for many sites

Forty stores, a head office, remote staff and a growing number of virtual networks in two regions: with plain VPN gateways you would manage dozens of connections, local network gateways and peerings, and build transit routing yourself. Azure Virtual WAN turns that into a managed service. You create a virtual WAN and a virtual hub in each region you use. A hub is a Microsoft-managed virtual network with gateways for site-to-site VPN, point-to-site (called User VPN) and ExpressRoute, plus a router that provides any-to-any transit: store to head office, store to VNet, VNet to VNet. Hubs in the same virtual WAN connect to each other in a full mesh over Microsoft's backbone. A secured virtual hub adds Azure Firewall for central inspection, and SD-WAN partners can automate store connections, so a new store's router builds its own tunnel.

Virtual WAN comes in two types. Basic supports site-to-site VPN only. Standard adds ExpressRoute, User VPN, transit between VNets and hubs, Azure Firewall and network virtual appliances. You can upgrade from Basic to Standard, but not back.

Tip: Don't reach for gateways when two Azure virtual networks just need to talk: VNet peering (Lunch 25) is cheaper, faster and needs no gateway. Use VNet-to-VNet VPN only when you specifically want IPsec between them — or, as in this lunch's lab, to rehearse a site-to-site connection without real hardware.

6. How it fits together for Nusantara Retail

Your recommendation to Ibu Sari comes in three phases:

1. Now — site-to-site VPN. A VpnGw1AZ gateway in active-active mode in the hub VNet (10.40.0.0/16, Indonesia Central), BGP with Pak Budi's firewall, and point-to-site with Microsoft Entra ID for the IT team. It's live within days and costs gateway hours plus outbound data.
2. Next quarter — ExpressRoute for head office. A Standard circuit with unlimited data, from a Jakarta peering location to Indonesia Central, for the nightly warehouse synchronisation. The VPN stays as the backup path. If the business later needs more, ExpressRoute Metro or a second circuit at another location raises resiliency.
3. When the stores join — Virtual WAN Standard. Each store's SD-WAN box connects to the Indonesia Central hub, a secured hub inspects store traffic, and the address plan from section 1 keeps every store clear of head office and Azure.

Ibu Sari's three questions now have answers. Private: the VPN encrypts traffic over the internet, and ExpressRoute stays off the internet (with encryption added where the data needs it). Resilient: active-active gateways, two connections per circuit and a VPN backup. Cost: mostly fixed hourly and monthly fees that you can estimate in the pricing calculator before signing anything.

Whatever you build, watch it. VPN gateways publish metrics such as tunnel bandwidth and BGP peer status to Azure Monitor, so you can raise an alert the moment a tunnel drops (Lunch 16). ExpressRoute circuits report availability and throughput, and Connection Monitor can test the path end to end, from a VM in Azure to a server at head office. The store whose upload failed three nights running would have raised an alert on the first night.

Pause and think: during the next 12.12 sale, head office's internet line drops for 30 minutes. With only the site-to-site VPN, what stops working? With ExpressRoute plus a VPN backup? And what would still fail if the whole head-office building lost power?

In Lunch 27 you move from the network edge to the storefront itself, with Application Gateway, Front Door and Traffic Manager.

Field notes from Stefanus

An untested backup path is only a rumour. Whenever a design says "VPN as backup for ExpressRoute", I ask two questions. First: when did we last fail over on purpose? I want a planned test in a quiet window — take the circuit out of service, watch the traffic move to the tunnel, confirm that the nightly sync still finishes, then move back. Second: how would we know we are running on the backup? A tunnel that quietly carries everything for weeks looks healthy on every dashboard, so I want an alert on the circuit itself, not just on the tunnel. Finally, I ask where the two paths physically meet. If both leave head office through the same router, the same power feed or the same cable trench, they are not two paths. They are one path with two invoices.

Go further

- Microsoft Learn: About gateway SKUs (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/vpn-gateway/about-gateway-skus) — current VPN Gateway SKUs, tunnel counts, throughput benchmarks and features.
- Microsoft Learn: VPN Gateway SKU consolidation and migration (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/vpn-gateway/gateway-sku-consolidation) — the move from non-zonal to AZ SKUs, with dates and FAQs.
- Microsoft Learn: What is Azure ExpressRoute? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/expressroute/expressroute-introduction) — circuits, peering, SKUs, billing models, Direct and Global Reach.
- Microsoft Learn: What is Azure Virtual WAN? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/virtual-wan/virtual-wan-about) — hubs, Basic versus Standard, and transit connectivity.

quiz.q: Pak Budi needs the warehouse server at head office to reach Azure privately by next week, on a modest budget. VPN or ExpressRoute?
quiz.a: A site-to-site VPN to a route-based gateway with an AZ SKU (for example VpnGw1AZ). It needs only an internet connection and a compatible device, while ExpressRoute needs a provider to provision a circuit, which takes weeks. Why: VPN is the fast, low-commitment way to start; ExpressRoute can follow later.

quiz.q: Rizky must reach a VM's private IP address from home, signing in with his Entra ID account and MFA. What do you set up?
quiz.a: Point-to-site VPN with Microsoft Entra ID authentication (OpenVPN and the Azure VPN Client) on a non-Basic, route-based gateway, with a client address pool that overlaps nothing. Why: Entra ID authentication brings MFA and Conditional Access to the VPN, with no client certificates to manage.

quiz.q: A colleague's script runs az network vnet-gateway create --gateway-type Vpn --vpn-type RouteBased … without --sku. A week later, enabling BGP fails. Why?
quiz.a: Without --sku the CLI creates a Basic gateway, and Basic doesn't support BGP. Create the gateway with an AZ SKU such as --sku VpnGw1AZ. Why: the CLI's default SKU is Basic, which is meant for dev/test only.

quiz.q: The finance team asks whether traffic on the planned ExpressRoute circuit will be encrypted. What do you answer?
quiz.a: Not by default. ExpressRoute is a private path that never crosses the internet, but it isn't encrypted. Use TLS in the applications, MACsec on ExpressRoute Direct, or an IPsec VPN over the private peering. Why: private and encrypted are different properties.

quiz.q: Forty stores, head office, remote staff and VNets in two regions need any-to-any connectivity, with a firewall inspecting store traffic centrally. Basic or Standard Virtual WAN?
quiz.a: Standard. Basic supports site-to-site VPN only; Standard adds User VPN, ExpressRoute, transit between VNets and hubs, and Azure Firewall in a secured hub. Why: any-to-any transit and central inspection are Standard features.

takeaways: Plan non-overlapping address space before you build any hybrid link — overlapping networks can't be routed.

VPN Gateway builds IPsec tunnels over the internet: site-to-site for sites, point-to-site (ideally with Entra ID) for people, VNet-to-VNet between VNets. In production use route-based, AZ SKUs, active-active and BGP.
Gateways take 45 minutes or more to create and bill every hour they exist; Basic is dev/test only and is the CLI's default SKU.

ExpressRoute is a private, predictable connection through a provider — not encrypted by default. Choose Local, Standard or Premium, metered or unlimited, and design resiliency with Metro, a second location and a VPN backup.
Virtual WAN Standard gives you managed hubs with any-to-any transit for many branches; Basic does site-to-site only.

lab.title: Connect head office
lab.text:
What you'll build

Pak Budi wants head office in Jakarta (10.0.0.0/16) to reach Nusantara Retail's Azure network (10.40.0.0/16) over a private, encrypted link instead of exposing servers to the internet. Nobody can ship a VPN appliance to your desk, so setup.sh simulates head office with a second virtual network that has its own VPN gateway: Azure plays both sides. You connect the two route-based VpnGw1AZ gateways with VNet-to-VNet connections in both directions, protected by a shared key generated at run time. Then you watch the status reach Connected, prove that vm-azure-1 and vm-hq-1 talk to each other on private IP addresses through the tunnel, and read the route Azure added. An optional task compares the result with VNet peering.

Caution: — the meter starts when setup.sh starts the gateways. A VPN gateway is billed for every hour it exists, whether or not any traffic flows, and this lab runs two of them (plus their public IPs and two small VMs). Do the lab in one sitting, never leave it running overnight, and run bash cleanup.sh as soon as verify.sh passes — or as soon as you decide to stop. For numbers, price a VpnGw1AZ gateway for your region in the Azure pricing calculator.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)). Contributor on the subscription is enough: this lab creates no role assignments.
- About two hours in which you can finish what you start. Most of the waiting happens at the beginning.
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. Nothing to install.
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/26-hybrid-connectivity
source ../common/config.sh
RG=$(rg_name 26)
PSK_FILE="$HOME/.azlunches-lab26-psk"

- Create the starting point. The script takes about 5 minutes:

bash setup.sh

setup.sh builds two "sites" in one resource group. Each gets a virtual network with a GatewaySubnet (/27, no network security group) and a workload subnet with an NSG, a small $VM_SIZE_SMALL VM without a public IP that runs a tiny web server, and a zone-redundant Standard public IP. Last, it starts a route-based VpnGw1AZ gateway in each network with --no-wait. The script finishes, but the gateways keep building in Azure for 30–45 minutes or more, even if you close Cloud Shell. Write down the suffix the script prints.

Important: Lab resources cost money while they exist. Finish with the Clean up section, even if you stop halfway — and even if the gateways are still building.

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–7 below (Task 8 is optional)
Challenge | you already know the basics | run setup.sh, read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Plan your time like this:

Clock | You | Azure
0:00 | run setup.sh (about 5 minutes) | creates the networks and VMs, starts both gateways
0:05 | Task 1: tour the half-built network | gateways building
0:15 | Task 2: read while you wait | gateways building
about 0:50 | Tasks 3–7 (and the optional Task 8) | gateways ready; the tunnel comes up within minutes
about 1:25 | verify.sh, then cleanup.sh | deletes everything in the background (10–20 minutes)

Task 1 · Tour the network while the gateways build

Look at what exists before the tunnel does — you'll compare it with the end result.

az network vnet-gateway list --resource-group "$RG" \
  --query "[].{gateway:name, sku:sku.name, generation:vpnGatewayGeneration, type:vpnType, state:provisioningState}" \
  --output table

az network vnet subnet list --resource-group "$RG" --vnet-name vnet-nusa-azure \
  --query "[].{subnet:name, prefix:addressPrefix || addressPrefixes[0], nsg:networkSecurityGroup.id}" \
  --output table

Now try to reach head office from the Azure VM. Run Command executes the script inside the VM through the VM agent, so you don't need SSH or a public IP. The first run takes a minute or two.

az vm run-command invoke --resource-group "$RG" --name vm-azure-1 \
  --command-id RunShellScript --scripts "ping -c 3 -W 2 10.0.1.10" \
  --query "value[0].message" --output tsv

Finally, look at the routes the network interface of vm-azure-1 uses. This takes up to a minute.

NIC_AZ=$(az vm show --resource-group "$RG" --name vm-azure-1 \
  --query "networkProfile.networkInterfaces[0].id" --output tsv)
az network nic show-effective-route-table --ids "$NIC_AZ" --output table

Tip: Prefer the portal? Home › Virtual network gateways lists both gateways while they build. For the routes, open vm-azure-1 › Networking, select the network interface, and choose Effective routes.

Checkpoint: both gateways show VpnGw1AZ, Generation1, RouteBased and the state Updating. The GatewaySubnet (10.40.255.0/27) has no NSG; snet-app has one. The ping reports 100% packet loss. The route table has 10.40.0.0/16 with next hop VnetLocal and 10.0.0.0/8 with next hop None — Azure drops traffic for private ranges it has no better route for, which is exactly what happened to your ping.

Task 2 · Read while you wait (30–45 minutes)

Each gateway is really a pair of Microsoft-managed instances that Azure places in your GatewaySubnet, spreads across availability zones and configures — one active, one on standby. That takes time, which is why real gateway changes are planned ahead and never done "just quickly". Check progress every ten minutes or so:

az network vnet-gateway list --resource-group "$RG" \
  --query "[].{gateway:name, state:provisioningState}" --output table

Use the time well. Each item below takes 5–10 minutes:

Read | Look for
About VPN Gateway SKUs (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/vpn-gateway/about-gateway-skus) | VpnGw1AZ's tunnel limit and benchmark throughput, and why the non-AZ SKUs are going away
Connect VNets with a VNet-to-VNet connection (Azure CLI) (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/vpn-gateway/vpn-gateway-howto-vnet-vnet-cli) | the steps setup.sh automated and the ones you'll do in Task 4; how it differs from site-to-site
Virtual network traffic routing (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/virtual-network/virtual-networks-udr-overview) | the None routes from Task 1, longest prefix match, and which route wins when two have the same prefix
What is Azure ExpressRoute? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/expressroute/expressroute-introduction) | the two peerings, and why a private circuit behaves more predictably than the internet
What is Azure Virtual WAN? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/virtual-wan/virtual-wan-about) | Basic vs Standard, and when forty stores make a managed hub the simpler design

Note: Cloud Shell closes after about 20 minutes without input. That doesn't affect the gateways — they build in Azure, not in your shell. When you come back, reload your settings: cd ~/azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/26-hybrid-connectivity && source ../common/config.sh && RG=$(rg_name 26) && PSK_FILE="$HOME/.azlunches-lab26-psk". In an ephemeral Cloud Shell session (no storage), clone the repository again and set SUFFIX=<the suffix you wrote down> before you source the settings.

If you'd rather watch than poll, az network vnet-gateway wait --resource-group "$RG" --name vgw-nusa-hq --created --timeout 4500 returns when that gateway reaches Succeeded — but keep the tab active so Cloud Shell doesn't time out.

Checkpoint: both gateways show Succeeded. If one shows Failed, see Troubleshooting.

Task 3 · Inspect the finished gateways

for gw in vgw-nusa-azure vgw-nusa-hq; do
  az network vnet-gateway show --resource-group "$RG" --name "$gw" \
    --query "{name:name, state:provisioningState, sku:sku.name, generation:vpnGatewayGeneration, vpnType:vpnType, activeActive:activeActive, asn:bgpSettings.asn}" \
    --output table
done

az network public-ip list --resource-group "$RG" \
  --query "[].{name:name, address:ipAddress, sku:sku.name, zones:to_string(zones)}" --output table

What you're looking at:

- VpnGw1AZ, Generation1 — the smallest zone-redundant SKU (up to 30 site-to-site tunnels). New gateways must use an AZ SKU; the old non-zonal VpnGw1–5 can no longer be created.
- activeActive False — the default active-standby mode: one instance carries the tunnel and the other takes over during maintenance or a failure, after a short interruption. Production gateways usually run active-active.
- asn 65515 — the default BGP autonomous system number. This lab doesn't use BGP; the stretch goals do.
- The public IP addresses are what a real head-office device would connect to — and what Pak Budi would allow through his firewall.

Checkpoint: both gateways are Succeeded, VpnGw1AZ, Generation1, RouteBased, with activeActive False and ASN 65515. Both public IPs are Standard with zones ["1","2","3"] (or null if you ran setup.sh with PIP_ZONES="" in a region without availability zones).

Task 4 · Create the connections with a shared key generated at run time

Both ends of an IPsec tunnel must hold the same pre-shared key. Generate a strong one in a file that only you can read, so it never appears on screen or in your command history:

[[ -s "$PSK_FILE" ]] || ( umask 077; openssl rand -hex 24 > "$PSK_FILE" )
ls -l "$PSK_FILE"

openssl rand -hex 24 produces 48 hexadecimal characters (192 random bits); letters and digits only, which every VPN device accepts. Now create one connection on each gateway. A VNet-to-VNet link always has two halves, and both must carry the same key:

az network vpn-connection create --resource-group "$RG" --name con-azure-to-hq --location "$LOCATION" \
  --vnet-gateway1 vgw-nusa-azure --vnet-gateway2 vgw-nusa-hq \
  --shared-key "$(cat "$PSK_FILE")" --output none

az network vpn-connection create --resource-group "$RG" --name con-hq-to-azure --location "$LOCATION" \
  --vnet-gateway1 vgw-nusa-hq --vnet-gateway2 vgw-nusa-azure \
  --shared-key "$(cat "$PSK_FILE")" --output none

With a VNet-to-VNet connection, Azure fills in the other side's address space for you. For the real head office you would instead create a local network gateway (Pak Budi's public IP and 10.0.0.0/16), connect to it with --local-gateway2, and type the same key into his VPN device — the stretch goals let you rehearse that.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Virtual network gateways › vgw-nusa-azure › Settings › Connections › + Add, connection type VNet-to-VNet, second gateway vgw-nusa-hq, then the same for the other direction. To paste the key without printing it in the terminal, open the file in the Cloud Shell editor: code "$PSK_FILE".

Checkpoint: az network vpn-connection list --resource-group "$RG" --query "[].{name:name, type:connectionType, state:provisioningState}" --output table shows con-azure-to-hq and con-hq-to-azure, both Vnet2Vnet and Succeeded. ls -l showed the key file as -rw-------. Anyone with enough rights on a connection can read its key back from Azure (az network vpn-connection shared-key show), so treat access to connections like access to a secret.

Task 5 · Watch the tunnel come up

The gateways now run IKE: they agree on encryption algorithms and prove to each other that they know the same key without ever sending it. Then they set up IPsec security associations, and from then on every packet between the networks travels encrypted. Check the status:

for con in con-azure-to-hq con-hq-to-azure; do
  az network vpn-connection show --resource-group "$RG" --name "$con" \
    --query "{name:name, status:connectionStatus, protocol:connectionProtocol, bytesIn:ingressBytesTransferred, bytesOut:egressBytesTransferred}" \
    --output table
done

Repeat it every 30 seconds until both say Connected — usually within a few minutes. Or let the CLI wait for you:

az network vpn-connection wait --resource-group "$RG" --name con-hq-to-azure \
  --custom "connectionStatus=='Connected'" --interval 20 --timeout 900

Checkpoint: both connections show Connected with protocol IKEv2. You may see Unknown or Connecting first — that's normal. The byte counters are small until you send traffic in Task 6.

Task 6 · Send traffic through the tunnel

From Azure to head office — ping, then ask the head-office web server for its health page:

az vm run-command invoke --resource-group "$RG" --name vm-azure-1 \
  --command-id RunShellScript \
  --scripts "ping -c 4 -W 2 10.0.1.10; curl -s --max-time 5 http://10.0.1.10/health" \
  --query "value[0].message" --output tsv

And back from head office to Azure, this time fetching the home page:

az vm run-command invoke --resource-group "$RG" --name vm-hq-1 \
  --command-id RunShellScript \
  --scripts "ping -c 4 -W 2 10.40.1.10; curl -s --max-time 5 http://10.40.1.10/" \
  --query "value[0].message" --output tsv

Neither NSG has a single custom rule, yet the traffic gets in. The default rule AllowVnetInBound allows traffic from the VirtualNetwork service tag, and that tag includes address ranges connected through the VPN gateway. In production you'd tighten this: Pak Budi's whole network doesn't need to reach every Azure server.

Checkpoint: both pings report 0% packet loss (round trips of a few milliseconds). The first command ends with ok; the second prints a small HTML page that says Served by vm-azure-1. Run the Task 5 loop again: the byte counters have grown.

Task 7 · Read the route Azure added

NIC_AZ=$(az vm show --resource-group "$RG" --name vm-azure-1 \
  --query "networkProfile.networkInterfaces[0].id" --output tsv)
az network nic show-effective-route-table --ids "$NIC_AZ" --output table

Compare it with Task 1. There's a new route for 10.0.0.0/16 whose source and next hop are both VirtualNetworkGateway. The old 10.0.0.0/8 → None route is still there, but Azure uses the longest prefix match: for 10.0.1.10, the /16 route is more specific than the /8 one, so the packet goes to the gateway instead of being dropped. Everything else in 10.0.0.0/8 is still dropped.

Now check the other side yourself: get the network interface of vm-hq-1 the same way and look at its routes.

Checkpoint: on vm-azure-1, 10.0.0.0/16 is Active with next hop type VirtualNetworkGateway. On vm-hq-1, the matching route is for 10.40.0.0/16. You added no route table and no static route: the gateways did it, and they would update the routes automatically if either address space changed.

Task 8 (optional) · Compare with VNet peering

Both "sites" are really Azure virtual networks, and between Azure networks VNet peering is usually the better tool: no gateways, no encryption overhead, lower latency, and you pay per GB instead of per gateway hour. Peer them while the VPN is still up and see which path Azure picks:

az network vnet peering create --resource-group "$RG" --name peer-azure-to-hq \
  --vnet-name vnet-nusa-azure --remote-vnet vnet-nusa-hq --allow-vnet-access true --output none
az network vnet peering create --resource-group "$RG" --name peer-hq-to-azure \
  --vnet-name vnet-nusa-hq --remote-vnet vnet-nusa-azure --allow-vnet-access true --output none

az network nic show-effective-route-table --ids "$NIC_AZ" --output table
az vm run-command invoke --resource-group "$RG" --name vm-azure-1 \
  --command-id RunShellScript --scripts "ping -c 4 -W 2 10.0.1.10" \
  --query "value[0].message" --output tsv

The CLI needs --allow-vnet-access true written out — its default for this flag is false. A peering only works when both directions exist.

Checkpoint: there are now two routes for 10.0.0.0/16. The virtual network peering route is Active and the gateway route is Invalid: Azure prefers system routes for peerings, even over gateway routes for the same prefix. Compare the time= values of the pings with Task 6 — they're usually a little lower.

Remove the peering before you continue — verify.sh checks that traffic uses the tunnel:

az network vnet peering delete --resource-group "$RG" --vnet-name vnet-nusa-azure --name peer-azure-to-hq
az network vnet peering delete --resource-group "$RG" --vnet-name vnet-nusa-hq --name peer-hq-to-azure

Break it and fix it

The most common reason a real tunnel never comes up is a mismatched pre-shared key — someone mistyped it on the device or rotated it on only one side. Give the head-office half a different key:

az network vpn-connection shared-key update --resource-group "$RG" \
  --connection-name con-hq-to-azure --value "NotTheRightKey123" --output none

Run the status loop from Task 5 for the next few minutes, then repeat the first ping from Task 6.

Symptom: the connections drop out of Connected (you may see Connecting or NotConnected) and the ping reports 100% packet loss. Nothing else changed — the gateways, routes and NSGs are all fine.

Hint: what went wrong, and the fix

During IKE each side proves that it knows the key. The keys differ, so authentication fails and no IPsec security associations are created; without them, no traffic can flow. Put the right key back on the head-office half:

az network vpn-connection shared-key update --resource-group "$RG" \
  --connection-name con-hq-to-azure --value "$(cat "$PSK_FILE")" --output none

Within a few minutes both connections are Connected again and the ping works. With a real device you would compare its IKE logs with the Azure side; Network Watcher's VPN troubleshoot tells you when the cause is an authentication failure.

If the status still says Connected a good five minutes after you set the wrong key, the old security associations are still alive. Force a new negotiation with az network vnet-gateway reset --resource-group "$RG" --name vgw-nusa-hq (it takes several minutes), and then watch the failure appear.

Verify your work

bash verify.sh

Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit. The script reads the effective routes and runs a small ping and HTTP test inside each VM through Run Command, so it takes 2–3 minutes. Remove the optional peering from Task 8 first.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

The script asks for confirmation (set ASSUME_YES=1 to skip the question). It deletes the resource group rg-lunch26-<suffix> — gateways, connections, public IPs, VMs, disks and networks — and removes the shared key file ~/.azlunches-lab26-psk. Nothing was created outside the resource group.

Deleting the gateways takes a while, often 10–20 minutes, and billing stops when they're gone. Half an hour later, check that nothing is left:

az group list --tag lunch=26 --output table

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
A gateway's state is Failed | Creation hit a transient platform error | az network vnet-gateway delete --resource-group "$RG" --name <gateway>, then run bash setup.sh again — it recreates only what's missing
setup.sh fails while creating a gateway because of the SKU | You set VPN_SKU to a non-AZ SKU such as VpnGw1, which can't be created any more | Run it again without VPN_SKU, or use VpnGw2AZ–VpnGw5AZ
vpn-connection create fails with AnotherOperationInProgress or says the gateway isn't ready | A gateway is still building or updating | Wait until both gateways show Succeeded (Task 2), then retry
A connection stays Connecting or NotConnected for more than 10 minutes | The two halves have different shared keys | Set both to the key in $PSK_FILE with shared-key update (see Break it and fix it)
$PSK_FILE is missing after a Cloud Shell restart, but the connections exist | The file lived in an ephemeral session | Recover the key into a new file: ( umask 077; az network vpn-connection shared-key show --resource-group "$RG" --connection-name con-azure-to-hq --query value --output tsv > "$PSK_FILE" )
Status Connected, but ping reports 100% packet loss | A VM is stopped, the optional peering was deleted on one side only, or a custom NSG rule blocks the traffic | Check az vm get-instance-view power state, the effective routes (Task 7) and the NSG rules; remove leftover peerings
(Conflict) Run command extension execution is in progress | Another Run Command is still running on the same VM | Wait until it finishes, then retry — one script per VM at a time
verify.sh reports a next hop other than VirtualNetworkGateway | The optional peering from Task 8 is still in place | Delete both peerings (end of Task 8) and run verify.sh again
Cloud Shell timed out during a wait | 20 minutes without input | Reopen it, reload the settings (note in Task 2) and rerun the command; the gateways kept going
az group list --tag lunch=26 still shows the group long after cleanup | Gateway deletion is slow | Wait another 15 minutes; if the group remains, run bash cleanup.sh again

Challenge brief

Run bash setup.sh, then build the following any way you like (portal, CLI, Bicep):

1. vnet-nusa-azure (10.40.0.0/16) and vnet-nusa-hq (10.0.0.0/16) each have a GatewaySubnet of /27 or larger (setup.sh creates these; don't change the address plan).
2. vgw-nusa-azure and vgw-nusa-hq are route-based VPN gateways with an AZ SKU, in the Succeeded state, each with a Standard, zone-redundant public IP (created by setup.sh; you wait for them).
3. Two VNet-to-VNet connections, con-azure-to-hq and con-hq-to-azure, use the same shared key, generated at run time — never typed, printed or committed.
4. Both connections are Connected.
5. The network interface of vm-azure-1 routes 10.0.0.0/16 to the virtual network gateway (no peering in place).
6. vm-azure-1 and vm-hq-1 can ping each other and fetch each other's /health page, in both directions.
7. You can explain why the GatewaySubnet has no NSG and why the NSGs needed no new rules (not checked by the script).

Then run bash verify.sh. Stuck? Peek at solution.sh or switch to Guided mode. Then run bash cleanup.sh.
